source.title: Cost-Optimal Grouped-Query Attention for Long-Context Modeling
source.authors: Yingfa Chen; Yutong Wu; Chenyang Song; Z. Thai; Xing-Yu Shen; Xu Han; Zhi-Yuan Liu; Mao-Song Sun

record.tranche_reason: The study fits and evaluates language-model loss scaling across model sizes and GQA configurations, using its own model experiments rather than reproducing the original scaling-law procedures.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own loss-scaling fits and its stated finding about loss versus inference costs. Scaling-law claims cited from other studies, and downstream benchmark comparisons that do not test a predictable scale-to-task relationship, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: For each of 21 GQA head configurations, the study trains Llama-3-style models from 3M to 1.2B on SlimPajama at 20 tokens per parameter. It fits loss as a power-plus-constant in non-embedding parameters and reports R2 over 0.999. This is a new architectural setting with a direct result on V1. The rest of the paper optimises inference cost, not the scaling law.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely right but should lead with the main result. Common GQA configurations are highly suboptimal for long contexts, and one should use fewer heads with a larger model. At 128K, H=(8,1) at 1.8B matches Llama-3 GQA's loss at 1.2B with 50.8% less memory and 57.8% fewer FLOPs, with similar downstream scores. Loss vs N fits (R2 over 0.999) and a new power-plus-constant law in head count underpin the recipe.
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes GQA architecture and inference costs, rather than reproducing the original training-scaling-law procedures or compute-optimal training allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The head-count fit coefficients vary with model size and context length; fits with fixed KV-head count are reported as less accurate.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed base model size, LM loss follows a power-plus-constant in the number of attention heads, with diminishing returns. At 1K context the fits are 470M exponent −0.124, 680M −0.177, 1.2B −0.227, with R2 over 0.999. Across 1K/2K/8K context the exponents are −0.039 to −0.044. Fits at fixed nkv for a 150M model have R2 over 0.97. Head count also changes the parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss scales as a power-plus-constant in attention-head count, with coefficients that depend on model size and context length.

fits_no_version.finding: At 128K context, loss has no simple power-law relation to inference memory or FLOPs across GQA configurations. It can be predicted from loss-vs-N fits shifted for time-variant costs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss vs inference cost is not a single power law when attention configuration varies, even when loss vs N is.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The scaling experiments cover model sizes up to 1.2B; the authors say they cannot be certain results hold at larger scales and that they have not thoroughly ablated all hyperparameters. The fitted loss is not identified as held-out in the reported text, and uncertainty estimates are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Power laws in training tokens or training compute; whether the loss is held-out; scaling of N with data held non-bottleneck.
No test of small-run fits predicting much larger runs. The Llama-3 405B extrapolation is only cited (Appendix B).
The compute-optimal N/D split is not studied; the 20:1 ratio is adopted from Hoffmann et al.
Depth, width and aspect ratio at fixed parameter count are not varied. The aspect ratio is fixed per size from Pythia, and head changes alter the parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No test of downstream performance scaling with size or loss. Only two configurations matched at target loss are compared.
Exponent and split dependence on setup and fitting choices is not tested numerically.

missing.what: Authors state that non-embedding parameter counting gives more predictable scaling laws in their experiments. No numbers are given for the alternative counting.

Llama-3 GQA (1.2B) and H=(8,1) (1.8B) are matched at target loss 2.615. Common-sense averages are similar (45.7% vs 45.5%), but NIAH differs (90.9% vs 96.9% at 1–8K; 30.4% vs 46.0% at 16K). The matched loss is from the 8K-context fits, and the downstream models have extra 128K training, so this bears on V6 only weakly.
Relative loss difference across model sizes (150M–1.2B) and head configurations is flat (<1%) for context above 8K. The authors use this to extrapolate loss to longer contexts.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 and V7 links were removed. Head-count sweeps change the parameter count, so they are not fixed-N shape tests, and their coefficient variation concerns a head-count law rather than V7's N/D/C exponents or splits. Figure 2 shows loss-vs-N curves differing across GQA configs, but no numbers at equal non-embedding N are given, so V4 cannot be read off it. Tranche T3 rather than T2: it is the standard loss-vs-N fit applied in a new architectural setting.

versions.untested_parts: The paper fits loss against model size, but does not report a separate loss law in training tokens or training compute. It does not specify that the fitted loss is held-out loss.
The paper does not report a held-out extrapolation test showing that fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Its optimization concerns inference costs and GQA configuration, not the growth of loss-minimizing parameter and token counts with a training-compute budget.
The study varies attention-head configuration at fixed model size; it does not broadly vary depth, width, and other architecture details.
No other modality or general test of the same power-law form across training regimes is reported.
Downstream benchmarks compare two configurations but do not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.

The study reports variation and a stated extrapolation limitation for head-count fits. It does not test whether parameter/token/compute exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with the listed setup and fitting choices, or whether published laws disagree.

rows.subject: models across GQA configurations (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit language-model loss as a power-plus-constant function of non-embedding parameter count for each GQA configuration.

conditions.value: 20:1 tokens per parameter in most experiments

rows.measure: Fit of LM loss against model size using the power-plus-constant scaling function
rows.note: The paper says it uses non-embedding parameter count because it gives more predictable scaling. It does not identify the loss as held-out.
rows.check: The link and state are correct. Training tokens scale with N at 20:1 (the Chinchilla frontier), so data is not held non-bottleneck; this is a loss-vs-N law along that frontier. The loss is not identified as held-out. The range is about 2.6 orders of magnitude in N.

rows.subject: 470M model
rows.operation_detail: Fit LM loss as a power-plus-constant function of query-head count.
rows.measure: LM loss versus number of attention heads
rows.note: The authors report diminishing returns as head count increases. This measures head-count effects, not a broad sweep of depth, width, and architecture.
rows.check: This is loss vs query-head count, and adding heads adds attention-projection parameters (Section 5.4 says nh and nkv add parameters). So parameter count is not fixed: it is not a V4 shape test at fixed N. It is also not a V7 exponent or split in N, D or C. It is a new head-count law; see fits_no_version.

rows.subject: 680M model
rows.operation_detail: Fit LM loss as a power-plus-constant function of query-head count.
rows.measure: LM loss versus number of attention heads
rows.note: The authors report diminishing returns as head count increases.
rows.check: Same as r2: it is a head-count law with parameters not held fixed, and it does not bear on V4 or V7.

rows.subject: 1.2B model
rows.operation_detail: Fit LM loss as a power-plus-constant function of query-head count.
rows.measure: LM loss versus number of attention heads
rows.note: The authors say these fitted curves would intersect at around n_h = 8K, likely incorrectly, and therefore break down before that point; they report accuracy up to 128 heads.
rows.check: Same as r2. The predicted curve intersection near nh=8K concerns the head-count law, not V7's N/D/C laws.

rows.subject: 470M model
rows.operation_detail: Fit LM loss as a power-plus-constant function of query-head count at different context lengths.
rows.measure: LM loss versus number of attention heads
rows.note: The fitted coefficients vary with context length. The authors report that the relationship remains power-plus-constant across these lengths.
rows.check: Same as r2. These are head-count fits across context lengths with a shared constant of 1.53, not a V4 or V7 measure.

rows.subject: 150M model
rows.operation_detail: Fit LM loss against query-head count while keeping KV-head count constant.
rows.value: Power-plus-constant fits; R2 values over 0.97. Individual equations are flattened and ambiguous in the text.
rows.note: The authors describe these fits as notably less accurate than the fits in Appendix I and suggest the smaller model may explain the difference.
rows.check: Same as r2. These are head-count fits at fixed nkv for a 150M model, with R2 over 0.97. The flattened equations show coefficients near 1.7 and exponents near 0.03.

rows.subject: models across a subset of GQA configurations (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare LM loss with inference memory, inference FLOPs, and a hardware-aware combination of those costs.
rows.measure: Relationship between LM loss and inference costs
rows.value: The paper says loss has no simple relationship with inference memory or computational costs, but can be predicted by fitting loss against model size and transforming the curves for time-variant costs.
rows.note: This concerns inference costs, not the training-compute scaling law in V1.
rows.check: This concerns loss vs inference cost, not a version of the claim. It is correctly recorded under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Loss vs non-embedding parameters, 3M–1.2B, 20 tokens/param, 21 GQA configurations, 8K context
relationships.reason: Power-plus-constant fits in N have R2 over 0.999 for every configuration (r1). The loss is not stated as held-out.
relationships.display_finding: Power-law-plus-constant fits against non-embedding parameters achieved R² > 0.999 for all 21 configurations.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Loss varies systematically with query-head count and the fitted head-count curves differ across model sizes and context settings; the paper reports diminishing returns, but does not quantify whether all changes are small (r2-r6).
